props.title: 24 City
props.initialSlug: Factory closure weaves real & staged worker stories

sections.content: 24 City (2008) represents Jia Zhangke's masterful blend of documentary and fiction, chronicling China's rapid industrialization through the demolition of a state-owned factory in Chengdu. Like his earlier work Still Life (2006), Jia captures the human cost of progress through a hybrid approach - mixing real factory workers with performed monologues by actors like Joan Chen. The film's innovative structure mirrors the fragmentation of memory itself, similar to how Sans Soleil (1983) weaves personal and collective history into a meditation on time and place.

sections.content: The factory-to-mall transformation in 24 City echoes through other vital works about industrial decline and economic upheaval. Wang Bing's monumental West of the Tracks (2002) spends nine hours documenting the collapse of China's state industry, while Pedro Costa's In Vanda's Room (2000) intimately portrays a Lisbon neighborhood's destruction. These films share Jia's concern with how modernization erases working-class spaces and histories.

The hybrid documentary form Jia employs builds on techniques pioneered in films like Abbas Kiarostami's Close-Up (1990) and Agnès Varda's The Gleaners and I (2000). By blending real testimonies with fictional elements, 24 City questions how we construct historical memory. The film's approach influenced later works like Apichatpong Weerasethakul's Cemetery of Splendor (2015) and Robert Greene's Kate Plays Christine (2016). SUBHEAD: Memory and Urban Transformation

sections.content: The mall that replaces the factory in 24 City symbolizes China's shift from production to consumption, a theme that runs through contemporary Chinese cinema. Similar concerns emerge in Liu Jiayin's Oxhide (2005) and Oxhide II (2009), intimate family portraits set in Beijing's changing urban landscape. Jia's focus on individual stories within massive social change influenced filmmakers like Bi Gan, whose Long Day's Journey Into Night (2018) explores memory and modernization in dreamlike ways.
